title_original: Irving Penn and the Haute Couture of Photography
excerpt_original: At the Maison Européenne de la Photographie in Paris, "Penn & Fashion" brings together the images of a man indifferent to luxury yet haunted by clothes, as a painter is by his motif. L’article Irving Penn and the Haute Couture of Photography est apparu en premier sur Blind…

blocks.text: In 1943, Alexander Liberman, the art director of Vogue , hired a young man “reserved and meticulous, largely indifferent to the ostentation of luxury” to dream up ideas for the magazine’s covers. Born in 1917, Irving Penn had trained under Alexey Brodovitch, the legendary art director of the rival Harper’s Bazaar . Pascal Hoël, head of collections at the MEP and curator of the exhibition, describes him as “already steeped in a rich artistic culture, and deeply engaged with modernist painting and European Surrealism.”

In 1947, the magazine asked him for a group portrait of the twelve most photographed models in America. Most of them turned their heads during the exposure: the faces melted into a blur while the gowns stayed tack-sharp. That day, he met Lisa Fonssagrives. Alexander Liberman would come to regard her as “the subject of Penn’s greatest photographs.” The exhibition opens with this group portrait, 12 Models Moving Their Heads , printed large: at this scale, the audacity of the conceit can be savored as no book allows.

In the summer of 1950, Vogue sent him to cover the Paris collections. On Rue de Vaugirard, he set up in a studio bathed in natural light, received the gowns of Balenciaga, Lafaurie, and Rochas, and photographed them against an old theater curtain mottled with grays. “Once again, he dispensed with staging: no narrative, no superfluous accessories, nothing to divert attention from the essential line of the garment.” When the trip ended, he married his principal model, Lisa Fonssagrives, in London.

“He placed his models within a world entirely his own,” Pascal Hoël observes, “asserting his independence from the commercial forces that surrounded him.” In one of his most celebrated images, his future wife wears the Balenciaga cape. The pale fabric rolls over the shoulder in heavy folds, a black-gloved arm bends up toward the collar, and beneath the cape a black line runs to the bottom of the frame. Against the gray of the curtain, the silhouette stands out as cleanly as if cut with tailor’s shears.

blocks.text: Now and then, he slipped an incongruous detail into the frame. In Man Lighting Girl’s Cigarette , a half-empty bottle squarely blocks the view, and the model, cigarette to her lips, dissolves into a blur behind the glass. “Though the poses may at first appear classical,” the curator continues, “they often reveal an unexpected extravagance, reminding us that an artist stands behind the lens.” Yet his extravagance obeys its own rules: every departure is calculated, every whim weighed on an assayer’s scale.

The sittings took their toll. Bettina Ballard, then an editor at Vogue , recalled his “tense, anguished, soul-searching attack,” adding that “the mental torture to which he put both the mannequin and himself left [her] drained at the end of a sitting.” Pascal Hoël describes models forced to contend with “the maestro’s exacting standards and acute sense of detail.” A whole day of preparation often went into a late-afternoon shoot: Irving Penn worked to the slow, rigorous rhythm of a couture atelier.

Diana Vreeland, by then the former editor-in-chief of Vogue , gathered the great French couture of the early twentieth century at The Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York in 1973: Paul Poiret, Madeleine Vionnet, Gabrielle Chanel, Elsa Schiaparelli, and Madame Grès, among others. Standing before these pieces, Irving Penn later recalled feeling “a thrill I had not as a fashion photographer known before.” He then made a bolder move still: he sent the models home and kept only the clothes. In an unused gallery of the museum, he photographed the gowns on resin mannequins, “investing these silent forms with a palpable presence.”

blocks.text: The great Japanese designer Issey Miyake worked with him from 1986 to 1999, an ocean apart. He shipped his clothes to New York and received the Ektachromes back in Tokyo; he missed every shoot, and Irving Penn every runway show. Theirs was an epistolary novel, written four-handed. “Penn’s photographs allow me to see my own designs,” Issey Miyake explained. That eye, Pascal Hoël adds, encouraged him “to think about clothing independently of fashion.”

Without Irving Penn’s eye, Issey Miyake admitted, “[he] probably could not have continued to find new themes.” Between 1987 and 1992, the graphic designer Ikko Tanaka created more than sixty posters for the house of Miyake from their color photographs; the exhibition shows twelve of them, on loan from the Miyake Issey Foundation. If fashion photography is, in the curator’s words, “the encounter between two creative forces,” it found here its most “singular expression.”

Irving Penn also turned his eye from the dress to the face. For decades, he shot the beauty pages of Vogue , published full-page and in color. Conceived with Phyllis Posnick, his final fashion editor at the magazine, these images, Pascal Hoël writes, “often combine humor, playfulness, and echoes of Surrealism that recall his beginnings.” Red-Lacquered Lid (1994), a print that entered the MEP collection in 2020, offers an eyelid lacquered in vermilion, caught in a pincer movement between a mascara wand and the black nozzle of a tube.

In Beauty Treatment with Gauze Mask , a thermal mask treatment covers the model’s entire face; a bold brushstroke turns it into “a striking tribal visage, almost unsettling,” recalling “the bird-man he had photographed in New Guinea some three decades earlier.” Alexander Liberman called these pages “stoppers”: “images so visually arresting,” the curator explains, “that they prevent the reader from turning the page, reshaping our expectations of the beautiful.” At the MEP, visitors stop dead before the prints, transfixed by so much grace. The spell still holds.

blocks.text: “Penn & Fashion” is on view at the Maison Européenne de la Photographie , in Paris, France, through January 17, 2027. Curated by Pascal Hoël in collaboration with Frédérique Dolivet. The bilingual catalogue Penn & Fashion includes Pascal Hoël’s essay “Irving Penn: The Eye That Redefined Fashion Photography” and is available at the MEP’s bookshop .

Irving Penn is also on view at the Bourse de Commerce , “The World According to Penn,” through January 10, 2027, and at Galerie Thaddaeus Ropac , “Irving Penn, l’essence du portrait,” through January 30, 2027.
